# Modeling two markers and their spread together {#sec-multivariate-distributional-regression}














Every model in this book so far has been a story about the *middle*. Where does the tissue area sit at day 7? By how much does GFAP rise between day 0 and day 3? The spread of the animals around that middle was a single number, the `sigma` that `lm()` and `brm()` hand you at the bottom of the summary, or it was something a family decided for us. I kept pushing that number to the back of the page, and I told you each time that it would come back. This is the chapter where it does.

The question that brings it back is one you would ask at the bench before you ever opened R: **after ischemia, do the animals simply shift, or do they also scatter?** Those are different findings. If every animal moves by the same amount, the group average moves and the group gets no wider. If the injury hits some animals hard and others lightly, the average moves *and* the animals fan out, and that fanning is a result about the biology (how reproducible the lesion is, how variable the response of the glia) that a table of means cannot carry. A model that gives the spread no formula of its own cannot even ask the question.

Let me show you the numbers that started this. @fig-mvdr_spread plots every one of the 49 animals by day, for two outcomes you know well by now: the tissue area of the section, and the integrated density of GFAP. The grey bar on each day is the mean plus and minus the single standard deviation that a model with one `sigma` believes for every day. The orange bar is the mean plus and minus the standard deviation the day actually shows. Where the two bars have the same length, one `sigma` is honest. Where they differ, it is not.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# The two outcomes in one long table, with the animal's day and condition
spread_long <- rbind(
  data.frame(outcome = "Tissue area (mm²)", DPI_f = cell_data$DPI_f, Condition = cell_data$Condition,
             y = cell_data$Tissue_Area),
  data.frame(outcome = "GFAP integrated density", DPI_f = cell_data$DPI_f, Condition = cell_data$Condition,
             y = cell_data$Gfap_IntDen)
)
spread_long$outcome <- factor(spread_long$outcome, levels = c("Tissue area (mm²)", "GFAP integrated density"))
spread_long$x <- as.numeric(spread_long$DPI_f)

# Per day: the mean, the SD of the day, and the single pooled SD of an equal-spread model
day_summary <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(spread_long, spread_long$outcome), function(g) {
  data.frame(outcome = g$outcome[1], x = seq_along(levels(g$DPI_f)),
             mean = as.numeric(tapply(g$y, g$DPI_f, mean)), sd_day = as.numeric(tapply(g$y, g$DPI_f, sd)),
             sd_pooled = sigma(lm(y ~ DPI_f, data = g)))
}))

# Every animal as a point; grey bar for the single sigma, orange bar for the day's own spread
ggplot() +
  geom_linerange(data = day_summary, aes(x = x - 0.28, ymin = mean - sd_pooled, ymax = mean + sd_pooled),
                 color = "grey55", linewidth = 2.2) +
  geom_linerange(data = day_summary, aes(x = x + 0.28, ymin = mean - sd_day, ymax = mean + sd_day),
                 color = "#D55E00", linewidth = 2.2) +
  geom_jitter(data = spread_long, aes(x = x, y = y, shape = Condition), width = 0.09, height = 0,
              color = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.7, size = 2.2) +
  geom_point(data = day_summary, aes(x = x, y = mean), shape = 18, size = 3.5, color = "black") +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(SHAM = 17, MCAO = 16)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:5, labels = levels(cell_data$DPI_f)) +
  facet_wrap(~outcome, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Days post-injury (DPI)", y = NULL, shape = NULL) +
  Plot_theme + legend_none() +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 14))
```

This picture is drawn with `ggplot2` (`geom_jitter()` for the animals, `geom_linerange()` for the bars, as in @sec-linear-regression-assumptions) because the argument is about the *spread*, and a spread is only convincing if you can see the animals it is made of. A bar plot of the day means with error whiskers would show you the means moving and hide that the whiskers should have different lengths for different days; a bar with an asterisk would hide it completely. The design tip: when the claim is about variability, draw the variability twice, once as the model believes it and once as the data show it, and let the reader compare the two lengths.

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read this figure"}
Start with the points: each is one animal, and the black diamond is the mean of its day. Then compare the two bars of each day. A grey bar longer than the orange one means the single `sigma` is too generous for that day (the model would predict animals farther from the mean than any we saw). A grey bar shorter than the orange one means it is too stingy (the model is surprised by animals that are not surprising). Tissue area (left): the day-3 orange bar is about 2 times the grey one, and the others are shorter than it. GFAP (right): the day-0 orange bar is about 0.11 of the grey one and the bars of days 7 to 30 are about as long or longer. The mistake to avoid is reading a long bar on one day as noise to be averaged away: it is the day telling you something.
:::

The tissue area of the left panel is spread by about 3.1 mm² at day 3 and by 0.7 to 1.2 mm² on the other days, against the single 1.6 mm² that an equal-spread model reports. GFAP is the same finding with a different shape: the standard deviation grows from about 25 at day 0 to between 247 and 319 from day 7 on, while the single `sigma` sits at 235. The grey bar of the GFAP panel at day 0 even reaches below zero, which an integrated density cannot do: a first hint that, for this marker, one `sigma` is the wrong kind of statement and not only the wrong size. Two outcomes from the same animals, two different ways in which "the animals scatter" is not constant over time, and both of them were flagged in earlier chapters and left open.

## Giving sigma its own formula {#sec-mvdr-model}

Picture the thermostat of an incubator, with two dials. One sets the temperature you want. The other sets how much the temperature is allowed to wobble around it. Every linear model so far gave us a dial for the temperature of each day and a single, fixed wobble for the whole experiment. A [distributional regression]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"} gives the second dial a formula too: the wobble of each day is its own number, and the model estimates the means and the wobbles together. The word "distributional" says what changed in the point of view. We are no longer modeling one summary of the outcome (its mean) but the whole distribution, and a Gaussian has two parameters, so each of them can depend on the predictors.

For tissue area by day, with $i$ an animal and $d[i]$ its day, the model is @eq-mvdr-model.

$$
\begin{aligned}
y_i &\sim \text{Normal}(\mu_i,\, \sigma_i), \\
\mu_i &= \alpha + \beta_{d[i]}, \\
\log \sigma_i &= \gamma + \delta_{d[i]},
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-mvdr-model}

where $\beta_0 = \delta_0 = 0$ for the reference day (day 0, the shams), so that $\alpha$ is the mean of the shams and $\gamma$ the logarithm of their standard deviation. The first two lines are the model you know. The third line is the new dial. Two things about it deserve a word before any number.

The first is the logarithm. A standard deviation has to be positive, and a linear predictor can wander to any real number, so the model works on $\log \sigma$ and exponentiates at the end (the same move as the log link of the count models in @sec-count-regression). The second is what that does to the coefficients. On the log scale, adding means multiplying: if $\delta_3 = 0.69$, then $e^{0.69} \approx 2$ and the animals of day 3 are about twice as variable as the shams. So $e^{\delta_d}$ is a [ratio of standard deviations]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}, the quantity that answers "how much more do the animals scatter on day $d$ than at baseline?", and a ratio is the natural way to talk about a spread, because the bench never asks how many mm² wider a spread is, but how many times wider.

In `brms` the second dial is a second formula inside `bf()`: `bf(Tissue_Area ~ DPI_f, sigma ~ DPI_f)`. `DPI_f` is the day as a category, which gives each day its own mean and its own spread, with no straight line imposed (the lesson of @sec-linear-regression-assumptions). Since the two formulas are free to differ, I could model the spread with fewer or other predictors than the mean; here they match because the question is whether each day has its own spread.

### Priors for a spread

A prior for a log standard deviation is easy to get wrong, for the reason the warning in @sec-glm-intro gave for every link scale: a coefficient that looks timid can be enormous once it is exponentiated. So I derive the priors on the outcome scale (the book's way, @sec-priors-regularization). For the mean part I use what the shams taught us in @sec-linear-regression-assumptions, a section of about 14 mm² and changes over the course of the experiment of a few mm², so `Normal(14, 6)` for the intercept and `Normal(0, 5)` for the differences between days. For the shams' spread, `Normal(0, 1)` on the log scale says that the standard deviation of tissue area at baseline is most likely around 1 mm², and plausibly anywhere from 0.14 to 7.1 mm². For the *differences* in log spread between a day and the reference, I need to say how different two days' spreads may be before the data speak. @fig-mvdr_prior (left) shows the ratio of standard deviations that three priors allow (and its right panel what the chosen one implies for the tissue area itself): `Normal(0, 0.5)`, `Normal(0, 1)` and `Normal(0, 2)`.

Why a model of the spread and not a transformation? The reasons usually given are three. A logarithm stabilizes a spread that grows with the mean, but it does nothing when two groups have similar means and different spreads (it changes the scale of the means and leaves the difference in spreads where it was); it breaks at zeros; and it hides the spread when the spread is what you want to estimate. This chapter's question is the third. Gelman, Hill and Vehtari show the model of this section, a regression whose residual standard deviation depends on a predictor, fitted with a `brms` formula for `sigma` [@gelman2020]; Inchausti does the same for the dispersion parameters of his ecological models [@inchausti2023]; and McElreath's broader point is that a model is a generative story, so nothing obliges its noise to be constant [@mcelreath2020]. The syntax, a formula for every parameter of the response distribution, comes from `brms` itself [@brms; @burkner2018].

The reason to be strict with the priors is the link-scale trap of @sec-glm-intro in its sharpest form. A coefficient of $\log \sigma$ is added on the log scale and exponentiated, so a `Normal(0, 10)` that looks vague allows a ratio of spreads of $e^{10}$, about 22,000, and puts nearly all of its mass on ratios that no experiment could show. The coefficients of $\log \sigma$ are unbounded real numbers, so they get an ordinary normal prior centered at zero. A standard deviation *itself* is bounded below by zero, and it gets a prior with positive support instead (the exponential of @sec-multilevel-varying-slopes, which I use again for the NeuN mice at the end of this chapter). And the way to know whether a prior is sensible is the prior predictive check, simulating from the prior and looking at the outcomes and ratios it implies [@gelman2026; @mcelreath2020]. The narrowest prior of the figure, `Normal(0, 0.5)`, keeps ratios between about 0.4 and 2.7 with 95% of its mass; the sensitivity section uses it as the cautious end.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Priors of the model of the spread: means in mm2, the spread on the log scale
prior_spread <- c(
  prior(normal(14, 6), class = "Intercept"),
  prior(normal(0, 5), class = "b"),
  prior(normal(0, 1), class = "Intercept", dpar = "sigma"),
  prior(normal(0, 1), class = "b", dpar = "sigma")
)

# Prior predictive fit (priors only, no data likelihood), as in the earlier chapters
fit_prior_area <- brm(
  bf(Tissue_Area ~ DPI_f, sigma ~ DPI_f),
  data = cell_data, prior = prior_spread, sample_prior = "only",
  chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 123,
  file = "models/multivariate-distributional-regression_fit1.rds", file_refit = "never"
)

# Share of a prior ratio of SDs that lies between one quarter and four times, for each prior width
share_ratio <- function(s) pnorm(log(4), 0, s) - pnorm(log(1 / 4), 0, s)

# Share of simulated tissue areas between 0 and 30 mm2 under the chosen prior
sim_area <- posterior_predict(fit_prior_area, ndraws = 1000)
share_area_ok <- mean(sim_area > 0 & sim_area < 30)
share_area_neg <- mean(sim_area < 0)
```

I drew the left panel by hand with `ggplot2::geom_line()` because it is not a simulation but a known distribution (a normal on the log scale), and the point is to translate it into the language of the bench: the horizontal axis reads as "how many times wider". With `Normal(0, 1)`, the one I use, the ratio of a day's spread to the spread of the reference day has 83% of its prior probability between one quarter and four times, so I am allowing a day to scatter several times more or less than the reference, which is what the GFAP data showed in the first figure, and still not an absurd number. `Normal(0, 0.5)` keeps 99% of the mass in that range and would take real convincing to believe a ratio of 5; `Normal(0, 2)` keeps only 51% and lets a ratio of 50 in. I come back to all three in the sensitivity section, because with a few animals per day the prior on a spread is the one place where I expect it to matter.

The right panel is the usual prior predictive check of @sec-priors-regularization: simulate animals from the priors alone and look at what they would measure. It is honest about a weakness: a Gaussian does not know that an area cannot be negative, so the prior (like the model) puts 4.1% of its simulated areas below zero, and 93% between 0 and 30 mm². The curve is much wider than the observed areas, as a weakly informative prior should be, and its bulk is on areas that a section of a brain can have.

### Fitting it

Two fits, so that we can see what the second dial buys: the same means with a single `sigma` (the model of the chapters before this one, with one mean per day), and the distributional model.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# One mean per day and a single spread: the model of the earlier chapters
fit_area_common <- brm(
  Tissue_Area ~ DPI_f,
  data = cell_data,
  prior = c(prior(normal(14, 6), class = "Intercept"), prior(normal(0, 5), class = "b"),
            prior(exponential(0.5), class = "sigma")),
  chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 123, iter = 4000, control = ctrl,
  file = "models/multivariate-distributional-regression_fit2.rds", file_refit = "never"
)

# One mean per day and one spread per day: the distributional model of the chapter
fit_area_sigma <- brm(
  bf(Tissue_Area ~ DPI_f, sigma ~ DPI_f),
  data = cell_data, prior = prior_spread,
  chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 123, iter = 4000, control = ctrl,
  file = "models/multivariate-distributional-regression_fit3.rds", file_refit = "never"
)
```
:::






`parsnip` has no engine that models the spread: its linear-regression engines estimate one residual variance. The frequentist counterparts live in other packages. `glmmTMB` takes the second formula in its `dispformula` argument (for a Gaussian, the log of the standard deviation again), and `nlme::gls()` takes a variance function, `varIdent()`, that gives each level of a factor its own standard deviation relative to a reference level. Both are shown next to the `brms` fit.

The half-eye is the picture that suits a quantity as awkward as a standard deviation. I use `ggdist::stat_halfeye()`, as in @sec-bayesian-core-workflow, because the posterior of a spread is skewed, with a short tail on the left (a standard deviation cannot go below zero) and a long one on the right, and a single bar with whiskers would force you to read a symmetric interval into something that is not symmetric. The black crosses are the raw standard deviations, so you can see where the model is shrinking an estimate toward the others. A bar plot of the means with asterisks, the figure most papers would show for these data, contains no information about any of this.

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read this figure"}
**Panel A**: each blob is the plausible range of one day's standard deviation. Read the horizontal position (the size of the spread), then the width (how sure we are), then the tail on the right (a spread can be much bigger than its estimate, never much smaller). A day whose blob sits clearly to the right of the others is a day with a wider spread. **Panel B** puts the same thing in the unit the bench uses: a ratio to the baseline, on a log axis so that "twice as wide" and "half as wide" are the same distance from the dashed line at 1. If a blob is entirely right of the line, that day is more variable than baseline; if it straddles the line, the data cannot tell. The mistake to avoid is to read a day-by-day difference in the middle of two wide blobs as a finding: look at how much the blobs overlap.
:::













Read the left panel first. The animals of day 3 scatter with a standard deviation of 3.0 (95% credible interval 2.0 to 5.2) mm², against 1.1 (95% credible interval 0.7 to 1.8) at day 7 and 1.1 (95% credible interval 0.7 to 1.7) at day 14. In the right panel that is a ratio of 3.4 [1.6, 7.1] to the shams, while the ratios of days 7, 14 and 30 are 1.2 [0.6, 2.5], 1.2 [0.6, 2.3] and 1.4 [0.7, 2.8]: their intervals sit around 1, which says that, within what these animals can say, the shams and the animals of the later days scatter alike, and day 3 does not. Day 3 against day 7, which does not use the shams at all, is a ratio of 2.7 [1.4, 5.4]. The probability that day 3 has the widest spread of the five days is 99%.

::: {.callout-tip title="Frequentist equivalent"}
Both frequentist fits find the same pattern. In `glmmTMB` the standard deviation of the shams is 0.63 mm² and the ratio of day 3 to the shams is 4.6 (95% Wald interval 2.3 to 9.5), against 3.4 [1.6, 7.1] in the Bayesian fit; the `gls` fit, by REML, gives 4.6 (2.1 to 9.9), the same within rounding. They do not agree to the decimal, and the reason is the lesson of the chapter in miniature: the shams are only 7 animals, and a spread estimated from seven animals is a noisy number, which the data alone place near 0.63 mm² and which my prior, centered on 1 mm², pulls up to 0.87. The ratio, which divides by that noisy number, moves with it. The means agree to the first decimal (day 3 minus day 0: 2.34 mm² in `glmmTMB`, 2.26 in `brms`, within 0.1 mm²). So the two lenses agree about *where* the spread changes and differ about *by how much*, and the difference is where a prior and a likelihood disagree most: in the estimation of a variance from few animals. I come back to that in the next section and in the sensitivity analysis.

## How much can eight animals say about a spread? {#sec-mvdr-few}

Ask a colleague to pipette 10 µL eight times and tell you, from those eight volumes, how steady their hand is. You will get a number. Ask a second colleague for another eight and compare the two numbers: they will differ by a surprising amount even if the two hands are identical, because *a spread is a property of the whole scatter, and eight points are a very small scatter*. A mean uses all eight values to locate one thing. A standard deviation uses the same eight values to measure how far they are from each other, and that is a less well determined quantity. The usual rough rule is that the relative standard error of a sample standard deviation from $n$ roughly normal values is $1/\sqrt{2(n-1)}$ (the width of a chi-squared distribution, in other words). For the 7 shams that is about 29%, for the 8 animals of day 3 about 27%, and for the 12 of day 14 about 21%. (This is a standard result of sampling theory, which follows from the chi-squared distribution of the sample variance; I give it as such and not as a quotation from the books.) Compare that with the mean of a day, which you know to a few percent. @tbl-mvdr_sd_table puts the estimates of every day next to each other, for the classical interval (based on the chi-squared distribution, which assumes a Gaussian) and for the posterior of the model of the previous section.






::: {#tbl-mvdr_sd_table .cell tbl-cap='Standard deviation of tissue area (mm²) by day. The classical interval uses the chi-squared distribution of the sample variance; the posterior is that of the model with a spread per day. The last column is the upper limit divided by the lower limit of the posterior interval.'}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Observed SD and its classical 95% interval (chi-squared with n - 1 degrees of freedom)
obs_sd_day <- tapply(cell_data$Tissue_Area, cell_data$DPI_f, sd)
n_vec <- as.integer(n_day)
classical_lo <- sqrt((n_vec - 1) * obs_sd_day^2 / qchisq(0.975, n_vec - 1))
classical_hi <- sqrt((n_vec - 1) * obs_sd_day^2 / qchisq(0.025, n_vec - 1))

# Posterior median and 95% interval of the model with a spread per day
post_q <- apply(sd_area, 2, quantile, c(0.5, 0.025, 0.975))

# One row per day
sd_table <- data.frame(
  Day = levels(cell_data$DPI_f), Animals = n_vec,
  `Observed SD` = round(as.numeric(obs_sd_day), 2),
  `Classical 95% interval` = sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", classical_lo, classical_hi),
  `Posterior median` = round(post_q[1, ], 2),
  `Posterior 95% interval` = sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", post_q[2, ], post_q[3, ]),
  `Upper / lower` = round(post_q[3, ] / post_q[2, ], 1),
  check.names = FALSE
)
gt(sd_table)

The first thing @tbl-mvdr_sd_table says is how wide these intervals are: for every day, the upper limit is between 2.3 and 3.2 times the lower one. A spread estimated from 7 to 12 animals is known to within a factor of about two or three, not to a decimal. That is not a defect of the Bayesian model: the classical interval is just as wide, and the two agree on which days are loose and which are tight. The second thing is how close the two sets of intervals are: the posterior ones are shifted a little toward the middle of the prior, and nowhere does one method say something the other contradicts. The third is the direction of the shift. For 7 shams with an observed standard deviation of 0.68 mm², the posterior median is 0.87: the model does not believe that seven animals which happened to land close together are *that* close in truth. Small samples underestimate their own spread more often than they overestimate it, and a prior that is not too narrow takes some of that back. (A spread cannot be negative, so there is more room above an estimated standard deviation than below it, and the posterior has a long right tail; McElreath makes the same point about the posterior of $\sigma$ [@mcelreath2020], and the half-eyes of the previous figure have that shape. It is also why a symmetric interval, an estimate plus and minus two standard errors, is the wrong tool for a spread.)

What to do about it is modest advice. Use a weakly informative prior, as I did, so that the right tail is bounded by something other than the data. Share information across groups (partial pooling) when the groups can reasonably be seen as draws from one population, which the five days of this experiment are not, since a sham day and a day of ischemia are different conditions, so each day keeps its own spread here. And report the whole interval, which is what the table does [@mcelreath2020; @gelman2020].

### One unusual animal, or a wider day?

Now to the question that @sec-linear-regression-single-continuous left open. At day 3 one animal sits well below the others (the lone low point in @fig-mvdr_spread), and without it the standard deviation of that day falls but does not reach the other days'. Is day 3 a day on which animals genuinely differ more, or is it a day with one unusual animal? With eight animals the data cannot be asked to settle it, but they can be asked to bound it, and there are three ways to put the question to the model. The first is the model I already have. The second keeps all animals and gives the likelihood heavier tails, a Student-t (the tool of @sec-beta-robust-regression), so that one animal far from its group is allowed to be far without forcing the whole day's spread up. The third removes the animal. The animal has no known technical problem, as far as the records of the experiment say (no section out of plane, no staining failure), so I do *not* delete it from the analysis: the third model is a sensitivity analysis, not a correction, in the same spirit as the Student-t sensitivities of @sec-beta-robust-regression.

@fig-mvdr_day3 and @tbl-mvdr_day3 show the answer I can honestly give. The Student-t model estimates a `nu` with a posterior median of 15.6: the tails it needs are only mildly heavy, and since that one `nu` is shared by all days it cannot give day 3 a tail of its own, so it leaves the ratio of day 3 to day 7 where it was (2.7 [1.4, 5.4] for the Gaussian, 2.6 [1.2, 5.5] for the Student-t). Removing the animal (tissue area of 10.5 mm², the lowest of its day) does move it, to 1.7 [0.9, 3.4]. In none of the three does day 3 become as calm as day 7: the probability that day 3 is wider than day 7 is >99%, 99% and 93%. And in none of the three is the interval narrow. So the answer to the question of the previous chapters is: *both*. The one low animal accounts for a good part of the excess (the ratio goes from about 2.7 to about 1.7), and what is left, a ratio of 1.7 [0.9, 3.4], is compatible with anything from no excess at all to a threefold one. How much of the wider day 3 is a wider day and how much is one animal, with eight animals, remains a question for a bigger experiment.

The closest frequentist route to the Student-t model is `glmmTMB` with `family = t_family()` and a `dispformula`. I tried it, and it ends with a warning of false convergence and returns, to the decimal, the Gaussian estimates: with this little data per day, the likelihood has nothing to say about the tails, and the optimizer cannot tell. I would not report it. What a frequentist analysis usually does here is the third row of @tbl-mvdr_day3: leave the animal in and report the interval, or take it out and report the interval. The Bayesian version adds a prior on `nu` that keeps the tails from becoming arbitrary, and the freedom to look at all three and say how much the conclusion moves.
:::


## Mean and spread together: what changes in the predictions {#sec-mvdr-predict}

A weather service can tell you two different things about March. It can say that the *typical* temperature of a March day in your city is 9 °C, known to within a degree because it has decades of records. Or it can say that the temperature you will meet on a *particular* March day will be between 2 and 16 °C. The first is a statement about an average and the second a statement about one day, and the second is wider because it carries the day-to-day scatter on top of the uncertainty about the average. Every regression has both statements, and `brms` computes them with two different functions. `posterior_epred()` gives the uncertainty about the *mean* of a day, the climate. `posterior_predict()` gives where a *new animal* of that day would land, the weather, which adds the animal-to-animal scatter, `sigma`, to the first.

This is where giving `sigma` its own formula pays off most visibly. The uncertainty about the *means* is a statement about how well we know each day's average, and it barely cares how `sigma` is modeled (a bit, through the weights each animal gets). The prediction for a new animal is built from `sigma`, so a model with one `sigma` can only make a prediction interval of the same width for every day, and a model with a `sigma` per day makes it as wide as the day deserves. @fig-mvdr_predint draws both intervals for both models, day by day.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# One row per day to predict: a new animal of that day
newdays <- data.frame(DPI_f = factor(levels(cell_data$DPI_f), levels = levels(cell_data$DPI_f)))

# For one model: 95% interval of the mean (posterior_epred) and of a new animal (posterior_predict), per day
set.seed(123)
pred_summary <- function(fit, label) {
  e <- posterior_epred(fit, newdata = newdays)
  p <- posterior_predict(fit, newdata = newdays)
  data.frame(model = label, day = levels(newdays$DPI_f), x = seq_len(nrow(newdays)),
             mean = colMeans(e),
             mean_lo = apply(e, 2, quantile, 0.025), mean_hi = apply(e, 2, quantile, 0.975),
             new_lo = apply(p, 2, quantile, 0.025), new_hi = apply(p, 2, quantile, 0.975))
}
pred_all <- rbind(pred_summary(fit_area_common, "One sigma"), pred_summary(fit_area_sigma, "Sigma by day"))
pred_all$model <- factor(pred_all$model, levels = c("One sigma", "Sigma by day"))
pred_all$width_new <- pred_all$new_hi - pred_all$new_lo
pred_all$width_mean <- pred_all$mean_hi - pred_all$mean_lo
```

The figure puts two intervals on top of each other in each model because they answer different questions, and mixing them up is one of the commonest mistakes in a Results section. It is drawn with `ggplot2::geom_linerange()` at two thicknesses, the mean as a thick bar and the new animal as a thin one, and with the animals themselves underneath. A bar plot with whiskers would show one of the two intervals (usually a standard error of the mean, which is the narrow one) and let the reader read it as the other.

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read this figure"}
Read the thick bars first: they are how well we know the average of each day, and they are short and almost the same for both models, so the means are not what has changed. Then read the thin bars, which say where a new animal would fall. Grey, one `sigma`: the same length on every day, which means that on day 7 it covers every animal and more, and on day 3 it leaves some of the animals outside. Orange, a `sigma` per day: short where the animals are tight and long on day 3. A good prediction interval is one that covers about 95% of animals of that day; count the dots outside each thin bar. The mistake to avoid is to quote the thick bar when you mean to say where an animal will land.
:::













Look at day 3. With one `sigma` the interval for a new animal is 6.8 mm² wide, the same as on every other day, and 1 of the 8 animals actually seen on that day falls outside it (a 95% interval would be expected to miss about 0.4). With a `sigma` per day it is 13.6 mm² wide, 2.0 times wider, and 0 animals fall outside it. On day 7 the intervals go the other way: 6.6 mm² with one `sigma`, 4.8 with a `sigma` of the day. Meanwhile the interval of the *mean* of day 3 is 2.2 mm² wide with one `sigma` and 4.4 with a `sigma` per day: it widens too, because the mean of a day of eight scattered animals is less well known than the mean of eight tight ones. That is the sentence promised in @sec-linear-regression-multiple, that every interval of that chapter was slightly optimistic for day 3: the ones for the mean, a little; the ones for a new animal, a lot.

# Leave-one-out predictive comparison of the three models (the Student-t one has its own scale per day)
loo_common <- loo(fit_area_common)
loo_sigma <- loo(fit_area_sigma)
loo_t <- loo(fit_area_t)

# Table helper: elpd difference from the best model, its standard error, and the number of Pareto k above 0.7
loo_table <- function(ll, label = "") {
  cmp <- loo_compare(ll)
  k_bad <- sapply(ll, function(x) sum(x$diagnostics$pareto_k > 0.7))
  data.frame(Model = rownames(cmp), `elpd difference` = round(cmp[, "elpd_diff"], 1),
             `SE of difference` = round(cmp[, "se_diff"], 1), `Pareto k above 0.7` = unname(k_bad[rownames(cmp)]),
             check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL)
}
cmp_area <- loo_table(list("One sigma" = loo_common, "Sigma by day" = loo_sigma, "Sigma by day, Student-t" = loo_t))

## A variance that follows from the mean, or a variance of its own? {#sec-mvdr-implied}

Two pipettes sit on the bench. The label of the first says "accurate to 1 µL". The label of the second says "accurate to 2%". Ask each for 10 µL and the first is off by up to 1 µL (10%) and the second by 0.2 µL. Ask each for 1,000 µL and the first is still off by up to 1 µL (0.1%), while the second is off by 20 µL. The first pipette has an *absolute* error that does not care what you ask of it; the second has a *relative* error, a spread that is a fixed fraction of the reading. Biological measurements come in both kinds, and the model has to say which kind it believes.

That is what a family does and what a distributional model lets you choose. A [coefficient of variation]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"} (CV) is the spread divided by the mean, the "2%" on the label. A Gaussian with one `sigma` says the error is absolute. A gamma or a lognormal outcome says the CV is constant: the variance is a *consequence* of the mean, because both grow together (this is what @sec-glm-intro meant when it said that choosing a family is choosing a model for the variance). A Gaussian with a `sigma` per day says neither: the spread of each day is a quantity of its own, to be read from the data. GFAP integrated density is a good place to compare them. It is positive, its spread grows with its mean (the first figure of the chapter), and there is a biological reason to expect a relative error: an integrated density is a sum of many positive contributions (area times intensity), and sums of positive terms vary in proportion to their size.

I fit six models for `Gfap_IntDen`, two for each idea. The Gaussian with one `sigma` is the straight-line model of the earlier chapters (with a mean per day), and with a `sigma` per day it is the distributional model of the last sections. The lognormal says that the logarithm of GFAP is Gaussian; the gamma, with a log link, says the mean is multiplicative and the variance is the square of the mean divided by a `shape`, so that the CV is $1/\sqrt{\text{shape}}$ on every day. Each can also be made distributional: a `sigma ~ DPI_f` for the lognormal, a `shape ~ DPI_f` for the gamma, which lets the relative spread differ between days. For the priors, the outcome scale again: GFAP of the shams is around 70, and of the injured animals a few hundred to a thousand, so intercepts on the log scale are centered on `Normal(5, 1.5)` (about 150, with 95% of the mass between 8 and 3,000), and the log-scale differences between days are `Normal(0, 1.5)`, which allows a factor of 19. The Gaussian gets `Normal(100, 150)` for the shams and `Normal(0, 500)` for the differences. For a spread on the log scale, `Normal(0, 1)` for differences as before, centered so that the Gaussian's standard deviation is around 55 and the lognormal's `sigma` is around 0.5. I checked the outcome-scale consequences of these priors with prior predictive fits for the two families that are new here.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Priors of the six GFAP models: a mean part on the original scale (Gaussian) or the log scale (the other two)

prior_l_mean <- c(prior(normal(5, 1.5), class = "Intercept"), prior(normal(0, 1.5), class = "b"))

# Gaussian: one sigma, or a sigma per day (log scale)
prior_g_common <- c(prior_g_mean, prior(exponential(0.005), class = "sigma"))
prior_g_free <- c(prior_g_mean, prior(normal(4, 1), class = "Intercept", dpar = "sigma"),
                  prior(normal(0, 1), class = "b", dpar = "sigma"))

# Lognormal: one sigma, or a sigma per day; Gamma: one shape, or a shape per day (log scale)
prior_ln_common <- c(prior_l_mean, prior(exponential(2), class = "sigma"))
prior_ln_free <- c(prior_l_mean, prior(normal(-0.7, 0.7), class = "Intercept", dpar = "sigma"),
                   prior(normal(0, 1), class = "b", dpar = "sigma"))
prior_ga_common <- c(prior_l_mean, prior(gamma(2, 0.2), class = "shape"))
prior_ga_free <- c(prior_l_mean, prior(normal(2, 1), class = "Intercept", dpar = "shape"),
                   prior(normal(0, 1), class = "b", dpar = "shape"))

# Prior predictive fits (priors only) for the two families that are new in this chapter
fit_prior_ln <- brm(Gfap_IntDen ~ DPI_f, data = cell_data, family = brms::lognormal(), prior = prior_ln_common,
                    sample_prior = "only", chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 123,
                    file = "models/multivariate-distributional-regression_fit6.rds", file_refit = "never")

I drew panel A with `ggplot2::geom_linerange()` and the crosses because the question is a *comparison of four statements about the same quantity*, and an interval for each against the raw value is the most direct way to see which statement the data support. The log-log mean-variance plot in B and C is the old diagnostic of the variance-stabilizing literature, and its use here is that it turns two competing ideas (constant `sigma`, constant CV) into two lines that you can hold a ruler against.

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read this figure"}
**A**: for each day, find the black cross (what the day shows) and check which colored bars contain it. A model whose bar misses the cross on several days is making a statement the data do not support; a bar that is very wide is a model that is not saying much. **B and C**: each point is a day. Points that follow the dashed diagonal behave as if the spread were a fixed fraction of the mean (a constant CV); points that sit on the grey horizontal line behave as if the spread were the same whatever the mean. A cloud that follows neither is a spread with a story of its own, and that is where the distributional model earns its place. The mistake to avoid is to read the dashed line as a fit: it is a reference, drawn through the geometric mean of the five observed CVs.
:::













For GFAP the points of panel B lie close to the diagonal: the CV of the days runs from 0.20 to 0.48, so the standard deviation grows roughly as fast as the mean, as a constant-CV family would have it, and the grey line is very wrong at both ends (it is why the grey bar of the first figure reached below zero). For tissue area, panel C, the days are not on the diagonal: the CVs run from 0.05 to 0.18, the mean falls by almost half between day 0 and day 30 while the standard deviation barely moves, and day 3 stands out with both a high mean and a very high spread. In tissue area the spread is not a consequence of the mean; it is a quantity of its own, and a gamma or lognormal would impose on it a relation that the data do not have.

For GFAP, then, the choice is between "the spread follows the mean" and "the spread is free", and @tbl-mvdr_gfap_loo asks the predictive question: which model predicts a held-out animal best?

@tbl-mvdr_gfap_loo says that the best model is Gamma, and the useful question is how far the others are from it in units of their own standard errors: Gamma, shape by day (0.1 behind, standard error 1.7); Gaussian, sigma by day (2.5 behind, standard error 3.2); Lognormal (3.1 behind, standard error 1.1); Lognormal, sigma by day (4.4 behind, standard error 2.9); Gaussian, one sigma (15.3 behind, standard error 4.8). Read against those standard errors, the picture is this. The Gaussian with one `sigma`, the model of the earlier chapters, is clearly last, about 3.2 standard errors behind. The gamma is ahead of the lognormal by about 2.8 standard errors, which is a modest preference for it. And the gamma cannot be told apart from the gamma with a shape per day, nor from the Gaussian with a `sigma` per day (2.5 behind, standard error 3.2). So the honest summary is that a model of the spread, in any of its forms, predicts better than one `sigma`, and that the data do not strongly decide between a spread tied to the mean and a spread of its own. What does discriminate is what each model *allows*. The Gaussians predict 6.9% (one `sigma`) and 3.5% (`sigma` per day) of new animals below zero, which an integrated density cannot be; the lognormal and the gamma predict none, by construction. And the predictive check of the standard deviation (the share of replicates at least as variable as the real day, @tbl-mvdr_gfap_ppc) says where each model is out of step.

Three lessons from @tbl-mvdr_gfap_ppc. The one-`sigma` Gaussian puts the two calm days at the very bottom of what it expects: 100% and 100% of its replicated days 0 and 3 were at least as variable as the real ones, because a spread of about 235 is far too large for them, and it puts day 7 in the upper tail (7%). The lognormal and the gamma, whose spread follows the mean, get the *order* of the days right without having a parameter for it, and are comfortable on days 0, 7, 14 and 30. Their trouble is day 3: GFAP at day 3 is tighter than a constant coefficient of variation allows (the CV of that day is 0.20 against 0.34 to 0.48 on the others), and 97% and 96% of their replicated day 3s are more variable than the real one. That is the gap that the `shape ~ DPI_f` and `sigma ~ DPI_f` versions of these families exist to close. And the Gaussian with a `sigma` per day gets every day right at the price of a parameter per day and of negative predictions in the early days. That is the trade: a family spends one number to say that the variance follows the mean; a distributional model spends one number per group to say that it does not; and for GFAP the data are in between, which is why the leave-one-out table cannot choose.

### What each choice says about noise

I do not think one of these is the right answer in general, so here is how I choose. Use a family that ties the variance to the mean (gamma, lognormal, and their relatives for counts) when the measurement is a positive quantity built from multiplicative or additive-positive contributions, when the CV is roughly constant in the data (@fig-mvdr_implied, panel B), and when you want predictions that respect the zero. It is the simpler statement: one number, with fewer parameters to estimate from few animals. Model the spread (a `sigma ~ ...` or equivalent) when the spread is itself a finding, when it does not scale with the mean (panel C), when the outcome can be negative or is bounded in a way that no family reflects, or when the groups differ in spread for a reason that has nothing to do with their means (a day on which animals diverge). The two are not exclusive: the gamma and the lognormal in @tbl-mvdr_gfap_loo with a `shape` or `sigma` per day are the middle path, a spread that follows the mean *and* may differ between days. The books I lean on say the same in their own terms. A family is a hypothesis about the noise around the mean, not about the mean itself, which lives in the linear predictor [@mcelreath2020; @gelman2020]. For strictly positive outcomes whose spread grows with their size they point to a gamma or a lognormal with a log link rather than a Gaussian on the original scale [@gelman2020; @inchausti2023]. And the relations between the parameters and the coefficient of variation that I used above (for the gamma $1/\sqrt{\text{shape}}$, for the lognormal $\sqrt{e^{\sigma^2} - 1}$) are properties of those distributions that any of them will give you.

The precedent for a parameter other than `sigma` was already in the book. In @sec-beta-robust-regression, the beta model's precision `phi` got its own formula (`phi ~ surgery`), and the sham mice, tightly packed, and the ischemic mice, scattered, stopped having to share a precision. That was a distributional model. Any parameter of a family can have its own linear predictor, and @tbl-mvdr_params lists the ones that you will meet.

::: {.callout-tip title="Frequentist equivalent"}
The AIC table of the `glmmTMB` tab ranks the six models by maximum likelihood, on the same outcome scale. It puts the one-`sigma` Gaussian last by a wide margin (AIC 681), the lognormal in the middle (666.5) and the Gaussian with a `sigma` per day first (649.1), with the gamma (651.1) and the gamma with a shape per day (651.5) within about two points of it. That is not exactly the order of the leave-one-out table (there the gamma was first and the Gaussian with a `sigma` per day second), and the difference is the useful lesson: the models that model the spread are close to one another, and which of them wins depends on whether you count fitted likelihood with a penalty (AIC) or predictive accuracy for a held-out animal (LOO). `glmmTMB`'s `dispformula` is the frequentist twin of `brms`' `sigma ~ ...`, `shape ~ ...` and `phi ~ ...` (all of them are dispersion parameters in its language), which is why the same argument served the beta model, the Gaussian here and the gamma. Where the two lenses differ is, once more, in the interval for a variance from few animals: a Wald interval for a log standard deviation is symmetric on the log scale and uses a normal approximation that is crude with eight animals, whereas the posterior is skewed as the data say it should be.
:::


## Two markers, one model {#sec-mvdr-multivariate}

Take the shoe size and the reading score of a thousand children between 5 and 12 years old, and the two correlate strongly. Nobody believes that big feet help you read. Age is behind both: older children have bigger feet and read better. Now take only the seven-year-olds and ask again. The correlation shrinks to almost nothing, because once age is held fixed, a child with larger feet than the other seven-year-olds is no better at reading. The first correlation was a statement about *children of all ages mixed together*, and the second is a statement about *children of one age*. They are different questions, and a paper that reports the first when it means the second has an error nobody can find in the model, because it is not in the model, it is in the question.

GFAP and PDGFR-β are the shoe size and the reading score of this book. In @sec-eda-ggpairs and in the exploration part you saw that the two markers move together across the dataset, and I told you at the time that DPI was driving both, a confounder (@sec-eda-ggpairs and [the introduction to exploration](eda-intro.qmd)). Now we can ask the question properly: **once we account for the day, do the two markers still go together in an animal?** If the animal that is high on GFAP for its day is also high on PDGFR-β for its day, something at the level of the animal (the size of its lesion, the section that was cut, the staining of that batch) pushes both, and the two markers are not two independent experiments. If not, the markers respond to the injury each on its own.

### The correlation everyone computes, and the one that remains

I analyze both markers on the log scale. The reason is the one of the last section: both are positive integrated densities whose spread grows with their mean, so on the log scale the spread is much more stable (the standard deviation of log GFAP runs from 0.21 to 0.58 over the days, and that of log PDGFR-β from 0.37 to 0.70), and a Gaussian is a defensible description. It is also the scale on which the lognormal model of the last section lives, so a difference of 0.69 between two means is a doubling. I keep a `sigma` per day for each marker, because the day-3 story differs between them, as we are about to see.

### A model for two outcomes

Think of two dancers on a stage. The music, which here is the day, sets the choreography that both follow, and much of what they do is explained by it. What the residual correlation asks is whether their *small deviations* from the choreography still move together, one leaning left when the other does. A [multivariate regression]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"} puts the two markers into one model as a *pair*. Each marker gets its own formula for its mean (and, if you want, for its spread), and the two leftovers of the same animal are allowed to be correlated: the model describes how the pair varies together, not only how each marker varies alone. The correlation between the leftovers is the [residual correlation]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}, and it is exactly the quantity of panel B: the association that remains once the predictors of the model have been used. With $y_{1i}$ the log GFAP and $y_{2i}$ the log PDGFR-β of animal $i$, @eq-mvdr-mv is the model. @fig-mvdr-dancers is the picture to hold.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\begin{pmatrix} y_{1i} \\ y_{2i} \end{pmatrix} &\sim \text{MVNormal}\!\left(\begin{pmatrix} \mu_{1i} \\ \mu_{2i} \end{pmatrix},\, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i\right), \qquad
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i = \begin{pmatrix} \sigma_{1i} & 0 \\ 0 & \sigma_{2i} \end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} 1 & \rho \\ \rho & 1 \end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} \sigma_{1i} & 0 \\ 0 & \sigma_{2i} \end{pmatrix}, \\
\mu_{ki} &= \alpha_k + \beta_{k,d[i]}, \qquad \log \sigma_{ki} = \gamma_k + \delta_{k,d[i]}, \qquad k = 1, 2, \\
\rho &\sim \text{LKJ}(2).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-mvdr-mv}

The first line is the new idea: a two-dimensional normal distribution, in which the standard deviations of the two markers, $\sigma_{1i}$ and $\sigma_{2i}$, are the ones of the distributional models of the earlier sections (one per day, each marker its own), and $\rho$ is the correlation between them. The second line is the same pair of models as before, one per marker. The third line is the prior on $\rho$: the LKJ prior of @sec-multilevel-varying-slopes [@lewandowski2009; @mcelreath2020], with $\eta = 2$, which is mildly skeptical of correlations near $\pm 1$ and treats a correlation of zero as the most plausible before the data (it is the same prior, for the same kind of object; here it describes the leftovers of an animal and there the baseline and response of a mouse). In `brms`, the whole model is `bf(...) + bf(...) + set_rescor(TRUE)`: one `bf()` per outcome, added, and `set_rescor(TRUE)` is what asks for $\rho$ to be estimated (with `FALSE` the two models are fitted jointly but with the correlation fixed at zero).

A word on what this model does and does not buy. The means of each marker, by day, are the same as in two separate models: the correlation does not change where the days sit. What the multivariate model adds is $\rho$ itself, with its uncertainty, and the ability to predict the *pair* of values of a new animal, which two separate models cannot do (they would predict the markers as if they were independent). The priors for the means and spreads are those I used for GFAP on the log scale: `Normal(5.5, 1.5)` for the intercepts (the logarithm of about 250), `Normal(0, 1.5)` for the differences between days and, for the spread on the log scale, `Normal(-1, 1)` for the intercept (a standard deviation of about 0.4 on the log scale, which is a 40% spread) and `Normal(0, 1)` for the differences between days.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Priors for each of the two outcomes (the resp argument names the outcome), and for the residual correlation
prior_mv <- c(
  prior(normal(5.5, 1.5), class = "Intercept", resp = "lgfap"),
  prior(normal(5.5, 1.5), class = "Intercept", resp = "lpdgfr"),
  prior(normal(0, 1.5), class = "b", resp = "lgfap"),
  prior(normal(0, 1.5), class = "b", resp = "lpdgfr"),
  prior(normal(-1, 1), class = "Intercept", dpar = "sigma", resp = "lgfap"),
  prior(normal(-1, 1), class = "Intercept", dpar = "sigma", resp = "lpdgfr"),
  prior(normal(0, 1), class = "b", dpar = "sigma", resp = "lgfap"),
  prior(normal(0, 1), class = "b", dpar = "sigma", resp = "lpdgfr"),
  prior(lkj(2), class = "rescor")
)

# Two outcomes, each with a mean and a spread per day, and a residual correlation between them
bf_mv <- bf(lgfap ~ DPI_f, sigma ~ DPI_f) + bf(lpdgfr ~ DPI_f, sigma ~ DPI_f) + set_rescor(TRUE)
fit_mv <- brm(bf_mv, data = cell_data, prior = prior_mv,
              chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 123, iter = 4000, control = ctrl,
              file = "models/multivariate-distributional-regression_fit14.rds", file_refit = "never")

# The same model with the residual correlation fixed at zero (two separate models, fitted together)
bf_mv0 <- bf(lgfap ~ DPI_f, sigma ~ DPI_f) + bf(lpdgfr ~ DPI_f, sigma ~ DPI_f) + set_rescor(FALSE)
fit_mv0 <- brm(bf_mv0, data = cell_data, prior = prior_mv[prior_mv$class != "rescor", ],
               chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 123, iter = 4000, control = ctrl,
               file = "models/multivariate-distributional-regression_fit15.rds", file_refit = "never")
```
:::






The frequentist counterpart of a multivariate regression is `lm()` with a matrix of outcomes, `lm(cbind(y1, y2) ~ x)`, which fits one regression per outcome and keeps their residual covariance together. Its limits are worth saying: it gives each marker a mean per day, and one common covariance matrix for all days, so there is no day-specific `sigma` (`nlme::gls()` can model the variance by day for one marker at a time, but then the correlation between markers is lost; I know of no mainstream function that does both). `car::Manova()` would add a joint test that the days differ for the two markers together, which is not the question of this section, so I leave it out; and `parsnip` has no engine for several outcomes at once. There is a further limit that does not bite here: `lm(cbind())` is Gaussian throughout, so it cannot put a count and a Gaussian marker in one model, which a multivariate `brms` model can.

Both fits pass the sampler checks (the table at the end of the chapter lists them). The residual correlation between log GFAP and log PDGFR-β in `brms` is 0.32 (95% credible interval 0.03 to 0.55), against the raw 0.58. It is positive with a probability of 98%, and the model's evidence is for a moderate association, with an interval from barely above zero to more than half. The frequentist counterpart, 0.34 with a Fisher-z interval of 0.05 to 0.57, says the same. And the day means of the two markers moved by at most 0.03 (on the log scale) between the correlated and the uncorrelated fits, as promised: the correlation does not change where the days sit.

The correlation changes what the model predicts for the *pair*, and nothing else, and leave-one-out cross-validation can say so, because it can score the pair as a whole (the joint log score) or each marker alone. The two answer different questions: the joint score asks how well the model predicts the whole animal, both markers at once, and the per-marker score asks how well it predicts one marker. Report the one that matches your question.

@tbl-mvdr_loo_mv shows the pattern one would expect. For each marker alone the two models are the same (difference 0.2 and -0.2, standard errors 1.0 and 1.0), because the correlation does not enter the prediction of a single marker. For the pair, the model with the correlation is ahead by 3.0 elpd units against a standard error of 2.9: about one standard error, in the right direction, and not more than that with 49 animals. Differences of this size are within the noise of the estimate itself, so I read them as a tie that leans one way, and I give more weight to the posterior of the correlation and to the joint predictive checks below, which ask directly about the thing the correlation is for [@vehtari2017]. A caution: each of these fits has 3 observations with a Pareto k above 0.7, as models with a spread per day often do, so the differences are approximate.

             file = paste0("models/multivariate-distributional-regression_fit", 15 + i, ".rds"), file_refit = "never")
  # Keep the fit (for the sampler table) and the draws of the correlation
  list(fit = fit, rho = as_draws_df(fit)$rescor__lgfap__lpdgfr)

It is not a mechanism. It says that, within a day, an animal that is higher than its day's average for GFAP tends to be higher for PDGFR-β as well, and the biology could be what you like: the extent of the lesion in the section that was cut, how close to the lesion the section lies, the staining batch, a shared response of astrocytes and pericytes to the same signals. The model cannot tell these apart. What it does say is that the two markers are not independent measurements, and that a result about one is partly a result about the other: if you test a treatment on GFAP and on PDGFR-β and find an effect on both, you have less than two pieces of evidence. And the opposite reading is available too. A residual correlation of zero would have meant that, once the day is known, the two markers wander independently, so each carries its own information about the animal; a correlation near 1 would have meant that one of them is redundant with the other, which is the *collinearity* of @sec-linear-regression-assumptions in a new guise (two thermometers in one beaker).

### One correlation for all days is a choice

The model estimates a single $\rho$ for all five days. If the markers were tied on one day and not on another, that single number would be an average that describes neither. The honest sensitivity analysis is panel B of @fig-mvdr_rescor: a separate two-outcome model for each day. And it is a lesson in how little a day of 7 to 12 animals says about a correlation: the day-by-day medians run from -0.05 (day 3) to 0.54 (day 0), and the intervals are each about 1.0 units wide on a scale that runs from -1 to 1. Of the five day-wise intervals, 5 contain the all-days median and 0 exclude zero: there is no day on which the data single out a different correlation, and no day on which they can rule out either a value of zero or a value of 0.7. If I suspected that the correlation changes with the day (say, tighter later, when a glial scar has formed), the answer is a larger study or a model with a correlation that depends on the day, which `brms` does not offer for the residuals of a multivariate model. Here, one $\rho$ for all days is the simplest description that these data cannot reject.

::: {.callout-tip title="Frequentist equivalent"}
`lm(cbind(...))` gives 0.34 for the residual correlation, `brms` 0.32, and the Fisher-z interval and the credible interval cover almost the same range. The two agree because the means have enough data and the correlation is moderate; with fewer animals or a correlation near 1, the Fisher-z interval would be in trouble at the boundary, while the posterior respects the limits of $[-1, 1]$ by construction. The structural difference is what each can *include*: the Bayesian model carries a `sigma` for each marker and day and a correlation at the same time; the frequentist function carries one covariance matrix for all days. That is the difference between the two tabs, and for these data it did not change the correlation.
:::

### Joint predictive checks

A model of two outcomes can be asked about the pair. The check I want is the two-dimensional version of @sec-mcmc-model-checking: does the model make pairs that look like the pairs of the animals? I show two views in @fig-mvdr_joint. Panel A draws, for each day, the observed animals and 100 outlines from the model, each outline being the 95% ellipse that holds a new animal of that day for one posterior draw (the same device as the clouds of @sec-multilevel-varying-slopes). Panel B asks the question as a single number: the correlation of the two markers within a day, pooled over days, of the real animals against the same statistic in 2,000 datasets simulated from the model.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Ellipse that holds 95% of a bivariate normal cloud with standard deviations sd1, sd2 and correlation rho
ell <- function(sd1, sd2, rho, level = 0.95, n = 100) {
  t <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = n)
  r <- sqrt(qchisq(level, 2))
  data.frame(x = r * sd1 * cos(t), y = r * sd2 * (rho * cos(t) + sqrt(1 - rho^2) * sin(t)))
}

# 100 posterior draws; for each day the center, the two spreads and the correlation of one draw
set.seed(123)
sel <- sample(nrow(dr_mv), 100)
ell_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(levels(cell_data$DPI_f), function(k) {
  pre <- function(resp, what) if (k == "0") 0 else dr_mv[[paste0(what, resp, "_DPI_f", k)]]
  do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(sel), function(j) {
    i <- sel[j]
    mu1 <- dr_mv$b_lgfap_Intercept[i] + if (k == "0") 0 else dr_mv[[paste0("b_lgfap_DPI_f", k)]][i]
    mu2 <- dr_mv$b_lpdgfr_Intercept[i] + if (k == "0") 0 else dr_mv[[paste0("b_lpdgfr_DPI_f", k)]][i]
    s1 <- exp(dr_mv$b_sigma_lgfap_Intercept[i] + if (k == "0") 0 else dr_mv[[paste0("b_sigma_lgfap_DPI_f", k)]][i])
    s2 <- exp(dr_mv$b_sigma_lpdgfr_Intercept[i] + if (k == "0") 0 else dr_mv[[paste0("b_sigma_lpdgfr_DPI_f", k)]][i])
    e <- ell(s1, s2, dr_mv$rescor__lgfap__lpdgfr[i])
    data.frame(day = k, draw = j, x = mu1 + e$x, y = mu2 + e$y)
  }))
}))

# Pooled within-day correlation, for the real data and for 2000 replicated datasets (draws x animals x markers)
within_cor <- function(y1, y2, day) {
  r1 <- y1 - ave(y1, day); r2 <- y2 - ave(y2, day)
  sum(r1 * r2) / sqrt(sum(r1^2) * sum(r2^2))
}
yrep_mv <- posterior_predict(fit_mv, ndraws = 2000)

stat_obs <- within_cor(cell_data$lgfap, cell_data$lpdgfr, cell_data$DPI_f)

## A variance with levels: do injured mice differ more? {#sec-mvdr-neun}

There is one more place where the book left the variance as a single number, and it is subtler than the others because the variance in question is not the residual of an observation but the spread of an *effect between animals*. In @sec-multilevel-varying-slopes every mouse had its own left-minus-right contrast in NeuN-positive neuron density, and the model learned how much those contrasts differ from mouse to mouse: a standard deviation, $\tau_z$, shared by all days. I ended that discussion with a warning that I can now cash in. The naive mice of 0 D have had no ischemia, and still their left and right cortex differ a little (the method has an asymmetry of its own), by an amount that varies from mouse to mouse. A single $\tau_z$ for all days mixes two different things: the scatter of the asymmetry that every mouse carries, and the scatter of the *injury response* on top of it. **Do the injured mice differ more from each other in their response than the naive mice differ in their asymmetry?** That is a question about a variance that depends on the day, and about a variance that sits one level up from the observations.

The data are the NeuN cortex regions of @sec-multilevel-varying-intercepts and @sec-multilevel-varying-slopes, prepared by the same rules, so I do not describe them again (@sec-neun-data has the description and the checks): cortex only, regions without a positive cell removed, the logarithm of the density as the outcome, 396 regions in 198 sections of 31 mice measured on one day each.

### One spread per day

Here is the model. It is the correlated varying-slope model of @sec-multilevel-varying-slopes, with one change: the pair of varying effects of mouse $k$, its baseline deviation $u_k$ and its response deviation $z_k$, no longer comes from one bivariate normal for all mice but from one *per day*, with its own two standard deviations and its own correlation. With $d[k]$ the day of mouse $k$:

$$
\begin{pmatrix} u_k \\ z_k \end{pmatrix} \sim \text{MVNormal}\!\left(\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix},\, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{d[k]}\right), \qquad
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{d} = \begin{pmatrix} \tau_{u,d} & 0 \\ 0 & \tau_{z,d} \end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} 1 & \rho_d \\ \rho_d & 1 \end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} \tau_{u,d} & 0 \\ 0 & \tau_{z,d} \end{pmatrix},
$$ {#eq-mvdr-neun}

and the rest of the model (@eq-slopes-model) is unchanged. The new quantities are $\tau_{z,0}, \tau_{z,5}, \tau_{z,15}, \tau_{z,30}$: the spread of the hemisphere contrast among the mice *of each day*. In `brms` it is one term, `(1 + hemi | gr(mouse, by = dpi))`: `gr()` is the grouping function and its `by` argument says that the standard deviations and correlations of the varying effects are estimated separately for each level of `dpi`. This is the "variance with levels" of the title: a variance (here, of the response between animals) that has a structure of its own. I keep the priors of the previous chapter for each of the standard deviations (`exponential(3)`) and the LKJ(2) for each correlation, and the residual `sigma` and the section-level spread stay common to all days, since the question is only about the mice.

A caution before the fit, which the books give and which this design makes pressing: a standard deviation for a subgroup that contains very few units is poorly determined, and five naive mice carry almost no information about a spread [@inchausti2023; @kruschke2015]. Two consequences follow. The standard deviations get a prior with positive support and fast decay, which the exponential is, and its rate deserves a sensitivity check (@sec-mvdr-sensitivity uses rates 1.5 and 6 around my 3; an `exponential(1)` would sit just outside the wide end). And the `gr(..., by = ...)` term is `brms` syntax [@brms; @burkner2018]; as far as I know the printed textbooks I rely on write such models in `lme4` or in Stan and do not use it.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Priors of the previous chapter: population level, residual spread, a standard deviation for every varying effect, an LKJ(2) correlation
priors_slopes <- c(
  prior(normal(6.7, 0.5), class = "Intercept"),
  prior(normal(0, 0.5), class = "b"),
  prior(exponential(3), class = "sigma"),
  prior(exponential(3), class = "sd"),
  prior(lkj(2), class = "cor")
)

# The model of the previous chapter: one spread of the mouse effects for all days
fit_neun_common <- brm(
  log_dens ~ dpi * hemi + (1 + hemi | mouse) + (1 | section),
  data = cortex, prior = priors_slopes,
  chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 123, iter = 4000, control = ctrl, save_pars = save_pars(all = TRUE),
  file = "models/multivariate-distributional-regression_fit21.rds", file_refit = "never"
)

# The model of this section: the spread of the mouse effects (and their correlation) for each day
fit_neun_by <- brm(
  log_dens ~ dpi * hemi + (1 + hemi | gr(mouse, by = dpi)) + (1 | section),
  data = cortex, prior = priors_slopes,
  chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 123, iter = 4000, control = ctrl, save_pars = save_pars(all = TRUE),
  file = "models/multivariate-distributional-regression_fit22.rds", file_refit = "never"
)
```
:::






The frequentist counterpart is the awkward part. `lme4` has no way to give a varying effect a different standard deviation per level of a group-level predictor. `glmmTMB` has: `diag(0 + dpi:left | mouse)` gives each day its own standard deviation of the hemisphere effect (uncorrelated with the mouse intercept, which stays common), so it is a simpler model than the Bayesian one. The third route is the one most people would take, one `lmer()` per day, which also lets the residual and section variances differ between days. Read panel A first. The spread of the hemisphere contrast among naive mice, $\tau_{z,0}$, is 0.09 (95% credible interval 0.00 to 0.38): not zero (the method's own asymmetry differs from mouse to mouse) and not well determined (five mice). Among the injured mice it is 0.17 (95% credible interval 0.03 to 0.41) at 5 D, 0.24 (95% credible interval 0.11 to 0.50) at 15 D and 0.12 (95% credible interval 0.01 to 0.27) at 30 D. The mice of 15 D are the ones that differ most from each other in their response: the lower end of their interval, 0.11, is above the naive median, and the ratio of 15 D to 0 D is 2.8 [0.5, 61.9]. But panel B is where the caution is. The probability that the spread at 15 D exceeds that of the naive mice is 88%, and the probability that the average spread of the three injured days does is 81%: these favor "injured mice differ more", but the ratios' intervals reach below 1 and above 10, because a standard deviation estimated from five mice, and one estimated from eight, are known to within a very wide margin. The dashed band in panel A is what the model of the previous chapter said: one spread for all days, 0.17 (95% credible interval 0.10 to 0.27). It was a compromise, a little high for the naive mice and a little low for 15 D.

So here is the answer I can give to the question that @sec-multilevel-varying-slopes asked. *Probably*: the response of the injured mice varies from mouse to mouse more than the naive asymmetry does, and the day with the most evidence is 15 D. The data are consistent with a ratio of about 2.8, and they cannot exclude one near 1 (12% of the posterior lies below it) or one as large as 60. A ratio is a poor summary here, because its denominator, the spread of five naive mice, has posterior mass close to zero, and dividing by something near zero produces enormous numbers. As a difference the same result reads: the spread of the response at 15 D exceeds that of the naive mice by 0.15 [-0.16, 0.42] on the log scale (median and 95% interval), with a probability of 88% that the difference is positive. I would write it as a hypothesis worth a larger group of naive mice, not as a finding. The cheapest improvement is more animals at 0 D, since five naive mice is the weak link, and every ratio of the figure divides by what they say.

::: {.callout-tip title="Frequentist equivalent"}
`glmmTMB` with `diag(0 + dpi:left | mouse)` fits the same idea in one model and lands in the same place for the injured days (its standard deviations are 0.02, 0.20, 0.21, 0.11 for 0, 5, 15 and 30 D), but it estimates the naive mice's spread at 0.02, essentially on the boundary at zero, where the Bayesian model, with five mice and a prior, says 0.09 with an interval from 0.00 to 0.38. The one-`lmer()`-per-day route gives 0.08, 0.17, 0.25, 0.14 and two of the four fits are singular (5D and 30D): the model has more variance parameters than a day of 5 to 10 mice can support, and it says so by hitting the boundary. This is where the two lenses disagree most in the whole chapter. A maximum-likelihood fit has no way to say "I do not know this variance, but it is not exactly zero"; the posterior does, and a variance estimated from five groups is precisely the case where that matters. The point estimates of the three approaches are of the same order, and none of them can show that the days differ.
:::

### How much does the prior decide?

With five mice, the prior on a standard deviation is not a detail. I refit the model of this section under three different priors for the standard deviations of the mouse effects, and that table is in @sec-mvdr-sensitivity, where it can be read next to the other prior choices of the chapter.


## Does the prior carry the answer? {#sec-mvdr-sensitivity}

Three times in this chapter I said that a variance estimated from few animals is the place where a prior matters most: the spread of day 3 from eight animals, the spread of the naive mice from five, and the correlation within a day. The check that keeps me honest is the one @sec-priors-regularization taught: refit under visibly different priors and see whether the conclusion moves. Three questions, three families of priors. For the spread of tissue area, the `Normal(0, s)` prior on the log-spread coefficients with a narrow (`s = 0.5`), the chosen (`s = 1`) and a wide (`s = 2`) width, the three of the prior figure. For the residual correlation, an LKJ with $\eta$ = 1 (flat), 2 (chosen) and 4 (skeptical). For the spread of the NeuN contrast among mice, an exponential prior on the standard deviations of the varying effects with rate 1.5 (wide), 3 (chosen) and 6 (narrow).






::: {.cell}

@tbl-mvdr_sensitivity is the table I would show a skeptical reviewer. For tissue area, the ratio of the spread of day 3 to the spread of day 7 is 2.4 [1.3, 4.2] under the narrow prior, 2.7 [1.4, 5.4] under the chosen one and 2.9 [1.5, 5.9] under the wide one: the order of magnitude is stable, and so is the finding that day 3 is the wide day, but the *size* of the ratio moves with the prior, as it should when each day is a handful of animals (a narrow prior shrinks every ratio toward 1, a wide one lets the data speak and the skew of the posterior grow). For the residual correlation, 0.34 [0.03, 0.57], 0.32 [0.03, 0.55] and 0.30 [0.03, 0.53]: an LKJ(4) pulls toward zero and an LKJ(1) lets it reach higher, but all three keep the median near 0.3 and the conclusion (a moderate positive residual correlation, smaller than the raw one). For the NeuN spread, the ratio of the response at 15 D to that at 0 D is 2.7 [0.5, 68.1], 2.8 [0.5, 61.9] and 3.2 [0.6, 77.5] under the three priors, and as a difference 0.15 [-0.21, 0.46], 0.15 [-0.16, 0.42] and 0.14 [-0.09, 0.37]. This is the row to read most carefully. The medians hardly move, which says the prior is not what produces the result, but the intervals are enormous for the ratio, because the denominator is estimated from five mice and can be close to zero, and for the difference they reach below zero under all three priors. The *direction* (injured mice at 15 D more variable than naive ones) is what the data lean toward under every prior, and its size is what five naive mice cannot pin down.

A sentence for a paper, then, that is honest about all this: "The standard deviation of tissue area at day 3 was about two to three times that of day 7 under every prior we tried (posterior median 2.4 [1.3, 4.2] to 2.9 [1.5, 5.9]), but its magnitude is uncertain by a factor of about two because each day contains only 7 to 12 animals." I would write the second half of that sentence every time.

## What the sampler said {#sec-mvdr-sampler}

Every fitted model of this chapter was checked against the three conditions of @sec-mcmc-model-checking (Rhat below 1.01, effective sample sizes above 400, no divergent transitions), and @tbl-mvdr_sampler lists them. A note for the day that you fit a model with a `sigma` per group and a group has only two or three animals: the log link lets the model push a spread toward zero, the likelihood becomes very steep when the animals of a group nearly coincide, and the sampler can diverge in that corner. I did not meet divergences here, but if you do, in this order: raise `adapt_delta` (to 0.99), put a prior on the log-spread coefficients that keeps the spread away from zero and from infinity (the `Normal(0, 1)` of this chapter does that), and, if a group is too small to support a spread of its own, let it share the spread of a neighbor instead of insisting on one.

## Reporting the results {#sec-mvdr-report}

The two results of the chapter, in the form a paper would carry them. They go with the rest of the sentences that the planned appendix on reporting will collect.

::: {.callout-note title="How to report it"}
**Results (distributional model).** The spread of tissue area was not constant across days. In the model with a standard deviation for each day, the animals at day 3 had a standard deviation of 3.0 (95% credible interval 2.0 to 5.2) mm², against 1.1 (95% credible interval 0.7 to 1.8) mm² at day 7 and 1.1 (95% credible interval 0.7 to 1.7) mm² at day 14 (shams, day 0: 0.9 (95% credible interval 0.5 to 1.7) mm²). The standard deviation at day 3 was 2.7 (95% credible interval 1.4 to 5.4) times that of day 7 (posterior probability that it was larger: >99%) and 3.4 (95% credible interval 1.6 to 7.1) times that of the shams. Without the animal with the lowest tissue area on day 3, the ratio to day 7 was 1.7 (95% credible interval 0.9 to 3.4). The means and standard deviations of the five days were estimated from 7, 8, 11, 12, 11 animals.

**Methods.** We modeled tissue area (mm²) with a Gaussian distribution whose mean and logarithm of the standard deviation each had a separate effect for each day (distributional regression in `brms`, `bf(Tissue_Area ~ DPI_f, sigma ~ DPI_f)`). Priors were Normal(14, 6) for the intercept, Normal(0, 5) for the mean differences between days (mm²), Normal(0, 1) for the log standard deviation of the shams and Normal(0, 1) for its differences between days. We fitted four chains of 4,000 iterations (2,000 warm-up); all Rhat were below 1.01, effective sample sizes above 400, and there were no divergent transitions. Compared with a model with a single standard deviation, leave-one-out cross-validation put the model with a standard deviation per day ahead by 9.8 elpd units (standard error 8.4), which does not separate them with 49 animals; the posterior predictive check of the standard deviation by day did. As sensitivity analyses we refitted the model with Student-t errors, without the lowest day-3 animal, and with narrower and wider priors on the log-spread differences.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="How to report it"}
**Results (multivariate model).** After accounting for the day, log GFAP and log PDGFR-β integrated density were positively correlated across animals (residual correlation 0.32 (95% credible interval 0.03 to 0.55), n = 49 animals; posterior probability that the correlation is positive: 98%). Without accounting for the day, the correlation was 0.58. Estimated within each day alone (7 to 12 animals), the correlation was too uncertain to say whether it changes with the day (95% intervals of at least 0.9 units in width).

**Methods.** We modeled the logarithm of GFAP and of PDGFR-β integrated density jointly with a bivariate Gaussian model (`brms`, `set_rescor(TRUE)`), with a mean and a logarithm of the standard deviation for each marker and day, and a single residual correlation with an LKJ(2) prior. Priors were Normal(5.5, 1.5) for the intercepts, Normal(0, 1.5) for the mean differences between days, Normal(-1, 1) for the log standard deviations of the first day and Normal(0, 1) for their differences. We fitted four chains of 4,000 iterations (2,000 warm-up), with all Rhat below 1.01, effective sample sizes above 400 and no divergent transitions. A posterior predictive check of the pooled within-day correlation and of the joint distribution of the pairs by day found no discrepancy, and the residual correlation was stable under LKJ(1) and LKJ(4) priors.
:::

## What to take with you, and what comes next {#sec-mvdr-close}

Four things. First, the spread of an outcome is a quantity with a formula of its own: `bf(y ~ x, sigma ~ x)` in `brms`, `dispformula` in `glmmTMB`, `varIdent()` in `nlme` [@nlme; @pinheiro2000], read on the log scale as a ratio of standard deviations. Second, a variance estimated from a handful of animals is a wide and skewed distribution, and the honest summary of a day-by-day spread says so; the interval, not the point, is the result. Third, a family that ties the variance to the mean (gamma, lognormal) and a model that lets the spread be its own parameter are two different statements about noise, and the data of this chapter showed one outcome for each: GFAP, whose spread follows its mean, and tissue area, whose spread does not. And fourth, two measurements on the same animal are not two experiments: the correlation that remains after the model has used the day (here about 0.3, against a raw 0.6) is the number that says how much one marker tells you about the other.

What the chapter did *not* do is let the days talk to each other. Every day here had its own mean and its own spread, estimated as if the animals of day 3 and the animals of day 7 knew nothing about each other, which is a fair description of a design with different animals on each day and a poor one of an experiment that follows the same animals through time, or of a glial scar whose course over thirty days is a curve, not five unrelated numbers. That is the job of @sec-longitudinal-timeseries: models for the whole course of the scar and for animals measured repeatedly, where the dependence between the sessions of one animal is part of the model, and where the spread over days can itself become a smooth function. And the values the microscope cannot see, the measurements below a detection limit or the animals with a missing section, are the subject of @sec-missing-data-measurement-error, where the variance of the *measurement* becomes one more thing to model.
